meta.audience: Readers of the abridgment; Mormon's brethren, the Lamanites
meta.location: Unstated; Mormon writes near the end of the Nephite nation

world_behind.title: A thousand-year jump, unannounced
world_behind.text: The previous page ended with Amaleki around 130 BC. This one opens with a man watching the destruction of his nation five centuries after Christ. The reader crosses a millennium between two chapters, and the only signal is the change of name.

world_behind.title: The wise purpose, unresolved on both ends
world_behind.text: Nephi was told to make the small plates "for a wise purpose" he did not know. Mormon includes them for a wise purpose he also does not know, and verse 7 says so outright. Two men separated by a thousand years both act on an instruction neither of them understands.

world_behind.title: An archival find
world_behind.text: Verse 3 has Mormon searching records already delivered into his hands and discovering these plates. The abridgment was finished down to Benjamin before he knew they existed. What the reader has been reading for six books is presented here as something its compiler stumbled on late.

world_behind.title: False prophets tried and punished
world_behind.text: Verses 15 and 16 report false Christs, false prophets, preachers, and teachers, all "punished according to their crimes." Religious offense is handled as a legal matter by the state, as it generally was in the ancient Near East, and the record does not describe the proceedings.

world_behind.title: A king who fights, judges, and preaches
world_behind.text: Benjamin swings a sword in verse 13, presides over punishments in verses 15 and 16, and labors with prophets to establish peace in verse 18. The portrait is of an office that has not yet separated its military, judicial, and religious functions.

words.text: An impersonal construction meaning it seems to me, and the King James Bible does not use it this way. Mormon says it supposeth him that his son will watch the nation die. The grammar holds the conclusion at arm's length, which is a strange thing to do with a sentence about your own child.

A shortening that preserves the substance. Treated at 1 Nephi 1:17. Mormon uses it of his own work. He is the first writer in the record to name his method. Everything from here to the end of the book is filtered through one man's judgment about what to keep, and he says so before the reader reaches it.

What is left over. Mormon uses it twice in two verses, both times for the part of his record still to be written, which he will take from the plates of Nephi. In the King James Bible the word is mostly what is left of an offering once the fire has had its portion, a leftover with rules attached to it. Here it is just the rest of a book, named by a man describing the shape of his work from the middle of it.

Selected, and therefore valuable. Treated at 1 Nephi 7:15. The word carries both. Mormon keeps the small plates because they are choice unto him and says he knows they will be choice unto his brethren. The allegory in Jacob 5 used it of the best ground in the vineyard. It is the record's word for what one keeps when there is no room for everything.

A plural noun for prophetic speech, and an uncommon one. The King James Bible has it once, in Paul's "Despise not prophesyings" (1 Thes. 5:20), and this record has it once besides, on Amaleki's plates (Omni 1:13). When Mormon says what these plates hold, he does not say history. He says prophesyings and revelations, and that is the whole stated reason he keeps them.

In Acts a dissension is a quarrel loud enough that soldiers have to break it up. Here it is a departure. The chapter reports "much contention and many dissensions away unto the Lamanites" (v. 16), and the little word "away" carries the meaning: these people are not arguing, they are going, and where they go is the enemy. Elsewhere in the record the dissenters are likewise people who left, sometimes the church and often the nation.

cites.quote: much contention and many dissensions away unto the Lamanites

spans.text: much contention and many dissensions away unto the Lamanites

phrases.term: May God grant that he may survive them, that he may write somewhat
phrases.text: A father's prayer for his son's survival, and the reason given is that the son may write. Mormon has already concluded his people will be destroyed entirely. What he asks for is a witness who outlasts them, and Moroni does.

phrases.term: I searched among the records which had been delivered into my hands, and I found these plates
phrases.text: The discovery is reported as ordinary archival work. He was going through what he already had. The small plates, Nephi's and Jacob's and the rest, enter the compiled record because a man doing an inventory noticed them, and the record says so plainly.

phrases.term: The things which are upon these plates pleasing me, because of the prophecies of the coming of Christ
phrases.text: The stated reason for keeping them, and it is a reader's reason rather than a historian's. Mormon is selecting on content he finds compelling, and the next clause explains why: he can see which of the prophecies have already been fulfilled from where he stands.

phrases.term: I cannot write the hundredth part of the things of my people
phrases.text: Jacob's formula, five hundred years later, now in the mouth of the man compiling the whole thing. The complaint that began as a frustration about metal has become the standing condition of the record, and from here forward it governs everything.

phrases.term: I do this for a wise purpose; for thus it whispereth me
phrases.text: To whisper is to speak below normal volume, and the verb measures the strength of the impression exactly: enough to act on, not enough to explain. This is the closest the record comes to describing its own composition as guided without explanation. Mormon gives a reason he cannot state, attributes it to the Spirit, and immediately concedes the limits of his knowledge. Nephi had been given the same instruction in the same words (1 Ne. 9:5).

phrases.term: I do not know all things; but the Lord knoweth all things which are to come
phrases.text: An admission placed in the middle of an editorial decision. Mormon is deciding what will survive, and he says he is working without full information. The sentence is a compiler describing his own position accurately.

phrases.term: That they may once again be a delightsome people
phrases.text: "Delightsome" means pleasing to look upon, and the record uses it of peoples rather than things; the phrase that carries the weight here is "once again," which makes the petition a restoration. This is Mormon's prayer for the Lamanites, offered by a man whose nation they are destroying. The petition is for their restoration and not for his people's survival, and it is the only thing in the chapter he calls a prayer.

phrases.term: Out of which my people and their brethren shall be judged at the great and last day
phrases.text: The plates given a judicial function. Preservation is requested in the previous clause and justified here, and the justification is that the writing will be read against both peoples at a final accounting. Memory is not the reason offered. Evidence is.

phrases.term: He did fight with the strength of his own arm, with the sword of Laban
phrases.text: Two strengths named together, and the second is a relic. Nephi took the blade in a dark street; Benjamin swings it in a war roughly four hundred and seventy years later. Across four books it has been a weapon, a pattern for an armory, a line in a eulogy, and now a king's blade. The record never explains how it was kept, only that it was.

phrases.term: There had been false Christs, and their mouths had been shut
phrases.text: The phrase is a New Testament one and the treatment is judicial. Mouths shut, punishment according to crimes. The account is administrative, and no argument with the false Christs is recorded, only the outcome.

phrases.term: They did use much sharpness because of the stiffneckedness of the people
phrases.text: Sharpness is severity of speech: Paul uses it of what he hopes not to need (2 Cor. 13:10), and Lehi used it defending Nephi to his brothers. Cause and method here, stated without apology. The record has defended harsh preaching before, at the end of Enos. Here it is attributed to many holy men at once and made a feature of Benjamin's reign.

phrases.term: By laboring with all the might of his body and the faculty of his whole soul
phrases.text: Body and soul named separately and both spent. The phrase occurs once in scripture. What it describes is the establishment of peace, and the labor is shared with prophets in the same sentence.

verses.label: v. 1–2
verses.title: A book written at the moment of handing over
verses.text: The record opens by giving its occasion, and the occasion is a transfer: "being about to deliver up the record which I have been making into the hands of my son Moroni." Verse 2 dates it loosely, "many hundred years after the coming of Christ," from a writer whose narrative elsewhere counts single years, and adds a prediction about the man receiving it: "it supposeth me that he will witness the entire destruction of my people." The whole book is written in the gap between one keeper putting the record down and the next picking it up.

verses.label: v. 3
verses.title: The plates were found after the work was done
verses.text: The discovery is reported as a sequence with a clear order: "after I had made an abridgment from the plates of Nephi, down to the reign of this king Benjamin... I searched among the records which had been delivered into my hands, and I found these plates." The abridgement already reached Benjamin when the extra plates turned up. What they contained is specified, "this small account of the prophets, from Jacob down to the reign of this king Benjamin," which is the run of short books a reader has just finished. The seam is explained by the writer standing at it.

verses.label: v. 5
verses.title: The measure the volume uses for what it left out
verses.text: The limit is stated as a fraction: "I cannot write the hundredth part of the things of my people." Six verses in the volume use hundredth part, at Jacob 3:13, Hel. 3:14, 3 Ne. 5:8, 3 Ne. 26:6, Ether 15:33 and here. Four different writers reach for the same figure. It is never varied to a tenth or a thousandth, and no writer ever explains where the number comes from.

verses.label: v. 7
verses.title: An editor who says he does not know why
verses.text: The reason given for including the small plates is not a reason: "I do this for a wise purpose; for thus it whispereth me, according to the workings of the Spirit of the Lord which is in me. And now, I do not know all things." Wise purpose stands in six verses of the volume, four of them in Alma 37 and one at 1 Nephi 9:5, always for a purpose the speaker cannot state; 1 Nephi 19:3 gives the plural, "other wise purposes." Whispereth occurs twice, here and at 2 Ne. 28:22, where it describes the devil. The most consequential editorial decision in the book is recorded as an impulse its own author could not account for.

verses.label: v. 10–11
verses.title: The chain of hands, and a prediction about it
verses.text: Two verses of the record trace the object itself: Amaleki delivers the plates to king Benjamin, who "put them with the other plates," and then "they were handed down from king Benjamin, from generation to generation until they have fallen into my hands." Verse 11 turns from history to a prayer and then to a claim: "I pray to God that they may be preserved... And I know that they will be preserved." The reason given is what is written on them, "out of which my people and their brethren shall be judged." A man who has watched his nation destroyed is confident about the survival of the object, and says nothing about how.

verses.label: v. 12
verses.title: Eleven verses about a book, ended by a dash
verses.text: The return to narrative is abrupt and the record marks it with punctuation rather than a transition: "And now, concerning this king Benjamin, he had somewhat of contentions among his own people." After a chapter given entirely to plates, purposes, custody and omission, the sentence that resumes the story is nineteen words long and contains no explanation of the change of subject.

verses.label: v. 15–16
verses.title: A list of what was put down, in one repeated formula
verses.text: Three categories of trouble are named and each is closed the same way: after false Christs, "their mouths had been shut, and they punished according to their crimes"; after "false prophets, and false preachers and teachers among the people, and all these having been punished according to their crimes." False Christs occurs once in the volume, in verse 15. The formula does the work that a narrative would, so a period of internal conflict is disposed of in two verses by naming its types and repeating the same phrase for its end.

chapter.title: The record explains its own construction and does not hide the seam
chapter.text: Mormon stops the narrative to say what he found, when he found it, why he kept it, and where the next section comes from. No other compiler in scripture is this explicit about the join, and the explanation is placed exactly where the sources change.

chapter.title: Two men act on the same unexplained instruction a thousand years apart
chapter.text: Nephi made the small plates for a wise purpose he did not know; Mormon attaches them for a wise purpose he does not know either. The record presents the whole arrangement as something neither participant could see the reason for.

chapter.title: The compiler admits the limits of his own knowledge
chapter.text: Verse 7 has him saying he does not know all things in the middle of the most consequential editorial choice in the book. It is an unusual sentence for an editor to preserve about himself, and he preserves it without softening.

chapter.title: The plates are described as evidence
chapter.text: Verse 11 makes the writing something both peoples are answerable to at the last day. That is a legal function, and it is a stronger reason for preservation than any the record has given before, stronger than the family, the genealogy, or the prophecies.

chapter.title: Mormon's only recorded prayer here is for his enemies
chapter.text: His nation is being destroyed by the Lamanites, and what he asks God for is that the Lamanites come again to the knowledge of God and be a delightsome people. Nothing is asked for the Nephites except that his son outlive them.

chapter.title: Benjamin is introduced by what he does
chapter.text: Verses 13 through 18 give five actions and no speech: he gathers armies, fights "with the strength of his own arm, with the sword of Laban," drives the Lamanites out, uses "much sharpness" against dissenters with the help of holy men, and establishes peace "by laboring with all the might of his body and the faculty of his whole soul." Not one word of his is quoted. The sermon at Mosiah 2 through 5 runs to four chapters, and everything the reader knows about the speaker before it begins comes from this list.

chapter.title: The chapter is written from the end and set at the beginning
chapter.text: The chapter is written from the end and inserted at the middle. Verse 2 has the writer stating that he has "witnessed almost all the destruction of my people," and verse 11 has him praying for the plates and then dropping the prayer for a certainty, "And I know that they will be preserved." Verse 7 supplies the reason for the insertion and concedes he does not have it, "I do this for a wise purpose... And now, I do not know all things." The same pairing of a stated ignorance with a stated confidence stands at 1 Nephi 9:5–6.

applications.title: Act on the whisper you cannot justify
applications.text: Mormon kept the plates on an impression he could not explain, and said so. When something small and unaccountable seems right, the chapter's model is to do it and note honestly that you do not know why.

applications.title: Say what you do not know
applications.text: He made a consequential decision and recorded that he lacked full information. In a report, a recommendation, or a piece of advice, name the limits of what you actually know.

applications.title: Search what you already have
applications.text: Mormon found the most valuable thing in his archive by going through material already in his possession. Before acquiring something new, inventory what is already on your shelf.

applications.title: Pray for the ones doing the damage
applications.text: Mormon's one prayer here is for the people destroying his nation. Name someone who has cost you something, and ask for their good specifically.

applications.title: Write so someone can be judged fairly
applications.text: The plates were kept as evidence. When you record something contentious, write it so that it would still be fair if read by everyone involved.

applications.title: Spend body and soul on peace
applications.text: Benjamin's labor is described as body and soul together, and what he produced was order rather than victory. Ask what the equivalent labor looks like in a conflict you are inside of.

questions.text: If I could ask one thing for the person who comes after me, what would it be?
What is already in my possession that I have never actually looked through?
When did I last act on an impression I could not explain, and what happened?
Who is costing me something right now, and could I pray for their good and mean it?
If what I write were read at a final accounting, what would I want to change about how I write it?
Am I using sharpness where patience is called for, or patience where sharpness is?
